newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece disappointed by refusal to return marbles.
newsitem.headline: Greece disappointed by refusal to return marbles.

text.p: Greek government officials expressed disappointment on Monday over a refusal by the new British government to return the Parthenon marbles to Greece.

"We are disapointed by comments from the newly elected British government. The Labour party had commited itself to return the marbles to where they belong," a senior government official, who asked for anonymity, told Reuters.

Britain's new Heritage Secretary Chris Smith ruled out returning the marbles to Greece despite a commitment by former Labour party leader Neil Kinnock that the classical sculptures, now housed at the British Museum, would be sent home.
"We decided it was not a feasible or sensible option. We won't do it," Smith told BBC television on Sunday.

The return of the marbles, brought to London nearly 200 years ago from Athens, has been a long-standing Greek demand, first put to the British government by the late actress and culture minister Melina Mercouri.
Hopes had risen in Greece that with Thursday's election of a new Labour government in Britain, the return of the treasures might now be closer at hand.
"It is our desire that this issue is brought up at a bilateral level with my British counterpart and the British ambassador in Athens," Culture Minister Evangelos Venizelos told reporters.
Smith, whose ministry is responsible for cultural affairs, said the marbles were an integral part of the British Museum collection, visited by millions of people each year.
"It would make no sense at all to split up the British Museum collection in that way," he said. An entire room in the museum is dedicated to the marbles.

The return of the 5th century BC artworks, known in England as the Elgin marbles after the British diplomat who removed them from the Parthenon in 1806, has been a highly emotional issue for most Greeks who feel that part of their cultural heritage was robbed.

"This is not about any cultural object," Venizelos said. "We are talking about sections that are necessary for the architectural and aesthetic unity of the most important monument of western civilisation."
He said that the Labour party had made an ethical and political commitment and that he would soon write a letter to the new British government, raising the issue again.

Lord Elgin made off with almost all the bas-reliefs from the Parthenon's frieze, most of its pedimental structures, and a caryatid from the Erectheion. He sold them to London's British Museum in 1816.
Smith said returning the sculptures could encourage other countries to demand the return of their treasures, thereby unleashing a worldwide swapping system of precious art works.
Those who oppose their return to Greece say the British Museum safeguarded them from damage while other sculptures at the Acropolis temples suffered Athens' notorious air pollution.
Greece has said it will build a new museum at the foot of the Acropolis hill to house them. The Italian-designed museum is scheduled to be finished in about three years.
